'''Leonid Berlyand''' is a [[USSR|Soviet]] and American mathematician, a professor of [[Penn State University]]. He is known for his works on [[asymptotic homogenization|homogenization]], [[Ginzburg–Landau theory]], mathematical modeling of [[active matter]] and mathematical foundations of [[deep learning]].

== Life and career ==
Leonid Berlyand was born in [[Kharkiv]], Ukraine. His father, Viktor Berlyand, was a mechanical engineer, and his mother, Mayya Genkina, an electronics engineer. He graduated from the department of [[mathematics]] and [[mechanics]] at the [[VN Karazin Kharkiv National University|V. N. Karazin Kharkiv National University]]. Then he obtained his Ph. D. degree from the same university. In his Ph. D. thesis, he applied the [[Asymptotic homogenization|homogenization theory]] to study of elastic composite materials. After his defence, he worked at the [[Semenov Institute of Chemical Physics]] in [[Moscow, Russia|Moscow]]. In 1991 he moved to the United States and started working at [[Pennsylvania State University]], where he has served as a full professor since 2003. He has held long-term visiting positions at the [[Collège de France]], [[Princeton University]], the [[California Institute of Technology]], the [[University of Chicago]], the [[Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in the Sciences]], [[Sorbonne University]], [[Heidelberg University]], [[Argonne National Laboratory|Argonne]] and [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos National Laboratories]]. His research has drawn support from the  [[National Science Foundation]](NSF),<ref>[https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=1628411&HistoricalAwards=false One of NSF-DMREF grants]</ref> [[NIH]]/[[NIGMS]],<ref>[http://grantome.com/search?q=@author%20%20Leonid%20Berlyand Berlyand's NIH/NSF grants]</ref> the [[Applied Mathematics]] Program of the [[United States Department of Energy|DOE]] Office of Sciences,<ref>[https://www.osti.gov/scitech/biblio/1340478 One of the DOE grants]</ref> BSF (the Bi-National Science Foundation USA-Israel)<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.bsf.org.il/bsfpublic/ListOfResearchGrants.aspx?PageId=451&innerTextID=451 |title=One of BSF gants |access-date=2017-12-03 |archive-date=2019-07-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190723020623/http://www.bsf.org.il/bsfpublic/ListOfResearchGrants.aspx?PageId=451&innerTextID=451 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and the [[NATO]] Science for Peace and Security Section. Berlyand has authored over 100 works on [[Asymptotic homogenization|homogenization theory]] and [[Partial differential equation|PDE]]/[[Calculus of variations|variational problems]] in [[biology]] and [[material science]]. He has organized a number of professional conferences and serves as one of two founding co-directors of the Center for Mathematics of Living and Mimetic Matter and the Center for Interdisciplinary Mathematics at [[Penn State University]]. He has supervised 16 Ph. D. students and 8 postdoctoral fellows.<ref>[http://concussion.psu.edu/faculty/ Berlyand on the site of the Sports Concussion Research Center at the Penn State University]</ref><ref>[https://sites.psu.edu/leonidberlyand/ Berlyand's personal page at the site of the Penn State University]</ref>

==Research==
Drawing upon fundamental works in classical [[asymptotic homogenization|homogenization theory]], Berlyand advanced the methods of homogenization in many versatile applications. He obtained mathematical results applicable to diverse scientific areas including biology, [[fluid mechanics]], [[superconductivity]], [[elasticity (physics)|elasticity]], and [[material science]]. His [[mathematical modeling]] explains striking experimental result in the collective swimming of [[bacteria]].<ref>L. Berlyand, M. Tournus, A. Kirshtein, I. Aranson. Flexibility of bacterial flagella in external shear results in complex swimming trajectories, Journal of the Royal Society Interface 12 (102) (2014) [http://www.personal.psu.edu/lvb2/pdf/TouKirBerAra14.pdf]</ref> His homogenization approach to multi-scale problems was transformed into a practical computational tool by introducing a concept of polyharmonic homogenization which led to a new type of multiscale [[finite elements]].<ref>H. Owhadi, L. Zhang, L. Berlyand, Polyharmonic homogenization, rough polyharmonic splines and sparse super-localization, ESAIM: Mathematical Modelling and Numerical Analysis. Special issue, 48 (2), pp. 517–552 (2014) [http://users.cms.caltech.edu/~owhadi/index_htm_files/ESAIM2014.pdf]</ref> Together with H. Owhadi, he introduced a "transfer-of-approximation" modeling concept, based on the similarity of the asymptotic behavior of the errors of [[Galerkin method|Galerkin solution]]s for two [[elliptic PDE]]s.<ref>[https://library.seg.org/doi/abs/10.1190/1.3627799 William W. Symes, Xin Wang. Subgrid wave modeling by transfer‐of‐approximation. SEG Technical Program Expanded Abstracts 2011: pp. 2909–2914]</ref><ref>[http://www.trip.caam.rice.edu/reports/2012/ThesisFinal_XWang.pdf X. Wang. Transfer-of-approximation Approaches for Subgrid Modeling, Ph. D. Thesis, Rice University]</ref>  He also contributed to mathematical aspects of the [[Ginzburg–Landau theory]] of [[superconductivity]]/[[superfluidity]] by introducing a new class of semi-stiff boundary problems.<ref>L. Berlyand, V. Rybalko. Solutions with Vortices of a Semi-Stiff Boundary Value Problem for the Ginzburg-Landau Equation, J. European Math. Society v. 12 n. 6, pp.1497–1531 (2009)</ref>

In 2020s Berlyand got interested in the rapidly developing area of [[deep learning]]. His focus has been on mathematical foundations of deep learning, specifically he addressed the mathematical issues of convergence and stability of training algorithms for [[Deep learning|deep neural networks]] (DNNs)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Berlyand |first1=Leonid |last2=Jabin |first2=Pierre-Emmanuel |last3=Safsten |first3=C. Alex |date=2021 |title=Stability for the training of deep neural networks and other classifiers |url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/10.1142/S0218202521500500 |journal=Mathematical Models and Methods in Applied Sciences |volume=31 |issue=11 |pages=2345–2390 |doi=10.1142/S0218202521500500 |arxiv=2002.04122 |issn=0218-2025}}</ref> and formation of [[Fixed point (mathematics)|fixed points]] of DNNs.<ref name=":0">{{Citation |last1=Berlyand |first1=L. |title=Random weights of DNNs and emergence of fixed points |date=2025-07-07 |url=http://arxiv.org/abs/2501.04182 |access-date=2025-07-21 |arxiv=2501.04182 |last2=Krupchytskyi |first2=O. |last3=Slavin |first3=V.}}</ref> Subsequently he worked on application of the [[Marchenko–Pastur distribution|Marchenko-Pastur distribution]] of [[Random Matrix Theory]] to [[Pruning (artificial neural network)|pruning]] of DNNs that drastically improves training efficiency.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Berlyand |first1=Leonid |last2=Sandier |first2=Etienne |last3=Shmalo |first3=Yitzchak |last4=Zhang |first4=Lei |date=2024-01-01 |title=Enhancing Accuracy in Deep Learning Using Random Matrix Theory |url=https://global-sci.com/article/91444/enhancing-accuracy-in-deep-learning-using-random-matrix-theory |journal=Journal of Machine Learning |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=347–412 |doi=10.4208/jml.231220 |issn=2790-203X|doi-access=free }}</ref> Berlyand also studied existence and stability of fixed points of [[autoencoder]] neural networks. This work was done in collaboration with his Ukrainian colleagues.<ref name=":0" /> In 2023 he published a textbook on introduction to mathematics of deep learning together with Pierre-Emmanuel Jabin.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Berlyand |first1=Leonid |title=Mathematics of deep learning: an introduction |last2=Jabin |first2=Pierre-Emmanuel |date=2023 |publisher=De Gruyter |isbn=978-3-11-102431-8 |series=De Gruyter Textbook |location=Boston}}</ref>
